newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stumps in Georgia, recycles education plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stumps in Georgia, recycles education plan.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday stormed into Georgia, the home state of Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich, with a plan to let 100,000 college students teach children to read.
"Forty percent of the eight-year-olds in America today -- 40 percent of them -- can still not read a book on their own ... If they can't read, they can't succeed," he said.

Hailing a recent "huge increase" in the college work study programme he achieved, Clinton added: "Today I propose that 100,000 of those work-study students join the 'America Reads' initiative and make up 10 pecent of those million volunteers we need."
The plan, which would enlist students receiving federally subsidised work-study college scholarships as reading tutors, requires congressional approval.

Clinton's stress on improving the reading skills of elementary school students -- a modest, low-cost initiative he first proposed back in August -- was in keeping with his strategy of stressing family values issues in the closing days of the presidential race, and ignoring attacks attacks by Republican challenger Bob Dole.

Dole and independent candidate Ross Perot have both blasted Clinton and the Democratic Party in recent days for taking questionable campaign contributions from foreign interests and a convicted drug dealer.

A small group of hecklers, who presumably were Dole supporters, held up a bed-sheet banner at the rally that said "Lie Detector," but people near them held up Clinton signs to keep it out of the television shots.

Clinton, way out in front of Dole in the polls and trying to run out the clock 10 days before the presidential election, wanted to capture Georgia's 13 electoral votes and help Democrat Max Cleland, a wheelchair-bound Vietnam veteran, in a U.S. Senate race.
Doug Sosnik, a White House political operative, said Clinton's visit might also help the Democrats win a congressional seat in the Macon area, where the president spoke later Friday.
Internal polls showed Clinton leading Dole in Georgia by five-to-10 percentage points, Sosnick said. It was one of four southern states that Clinton carried in 1992.

Although the Clinton campaign has tried to capitalise on Gingrich's unpopularity nationally, the president made no mention of the speaker at the downtown Atlanta rally. Gingrich represents an Atlanta suburb.

The outdoor rally was part of a day-long national get-out- the-vote push targeting younger voters, who in past presidential elections have had one of the lowest turnouts of any U.S. demographic group.
Michael Stipe, leader of the popular rock music band R.E.M., was among those introduced to the crowd.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton's plan to create an army of reading tutors was an issue likely to resonate with voters in the 25-to-35 year age bracket.

Making a direct appeal to younger voters, Clinton said "this is your election and we need you. You have most of your tomorrows in front of you. You have your future out there ahead of you, and you have to decide that."
While in Atlanta, Clinton also placed a telephone conference call to hundreds of black ministers in 32 states to urge them to get their followers to the voting booth on Nov. 5.
"The outcome will be determined by the turnout," he said. "Don't be fooled by the polls...You know what to do and how to do it."
African-Americans are an important Democratic Party constituency, but blacks have also turned out in relatively low numbers in recent elections.

Clinton was to take a rare day off from campaigning on Saturday to help his wife Hillary celebrate her 49th birthday in Washington. McCurry said the first couple had nothing special planned, but agreed that a quiet celebration would "be the most fun."
